value.overview: The Spectacled Petrel (Procellaria conspicillata) is a large, dark seabird of the South Atlantic. Its name comes from the bold white markings surrounding the eyes, which contrast with its blackish head and body. It breeds only on Inaccessible Island in the Tristan da Cunha group. Although its population has recovered from historical lows, the species remains vulnerable because its entire breeding population is concentrated at one small island and it faces risks at sea.
value.classification: The Spectacled Petrel belongs to the petrel family Procellariidae in the order Procellariiformes. It was once treated as a subspecies of the White-chinned Petrel but is now recognized as a separate species.
value.identification: This is a large petrel, about 55 centimetres long, with an overall dark brown to black plumage. Its most distinctive feature is the conspicuous pale or white pattern around the eyes, giving the impression of spectacles. The bill is yellowish with a darker tip. It can resemble a White-chinned Petrel, but the latter lacks the sharply contrasting eye markings. In flight, it shows long, broad wings and a powerful, gliding style typical of large Procellaria petrels.
value.rangeHabitat: Spectacled Petrels breed only on the high western plateau of Inaccessible Island in the Tristan da Cunha group, in the South Atlantic. Away from the colony, they forage over oceanic waters, mainly between South America and southern Africa, with many birds occurring off southern Brazil. They usually use open sea rather than coastal habitats. In Costa Rica, the species is an accidental visitor: the first national record was a fatigued individual found at Laguna Penitencia, Tortuguero, on February 24, 2022.
value.migrationStatus: It is a dispersive, non-breeding seabird rather than a conventional land migrant. After breeding, birds range widely across the South Atlantic. Costa Rica lies far north of the species’ usual range, and its presence there is exceptional; the Tortuguero bird in February 2022 was reportedly the first record for Costa Rica and the Northern Hemisphere.
value.breeding: Breeding is restricted to Inaccessible Island, where colonies occur in wet heath, bog fern heath, and areas of Phylica woodland at roughly 250–500 metres elevation. Spectacled Petrels nest in burrows and usually lay a single white egg. Both adults contribute to incubation and chick care. Breeding takes place during the austral spring and summer, with activity generally extending from about September through March. The species has high dependence on the security of its single breeding island.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of squid and other cephalopods, along with fish and crustaceans. Spectacled Petrels take prey from the ocean surface and by shallow dives. They may also follow fishing vessels to consume discarded fish or offal, behavior that can increase exposure to fishing gear. Feeding occurs over productive oceanic waters, including areas near continental shelf edges and waters used by commercial fisheries.
value.behavior: Spectacled Petrels are strongly marine and spend most of their lives at sea. They are powerful fliers that use dynamic soaring and can travel long distances over open water. Birds may gather around fishing vessels or food concentrations. At the breeding colony they are active in and around burrows, especially at night. Like other burrowing petrels, they have a single-chick breeding strategy and generally show strong attachment to their nesting site.

conservation.populationTrend: The breeding population has increased substantially since historical lows, following the disappearance of introduced pigs from Inaccessible Island. Recent estimates indicate tens of thousands of breeding pairs, but the population remains vulnerable because all birds depend on one small island.
conservation.threats: Incidental capture in longline fisheries, particularly in the South Atlantic, is a major at-sea threat. The species is also highly exposed to accidental events because it breeds at only one locality. The introduction of rats or mice to Inaccessible Island could seriously harm eggs, chicks, and adults. Marine pollution, changes in prey availability, and poorly managed fishing activity may add further pressure.
conservation.howToHelp: Support seabird-safe fisheries that use bird-scaring lines, weighted lines, and night setting to reduce longline bycatch. Protect Inaccessible Island through strict biosecurity, careful control of landings, and prevention of invasive rodents. In Costa Rica, report unusual sightings through established bird-recording programs and avoid disturbing exhausted seabirds; records can improve understanding of this rare accidental visitor.
